course.title: Cybersecurity Basics
course.tagline: Learn how attacks work and how to protect accounts, websites and small businesses.

days.title: What Cybersecurity Is
days.goal: Understand what cybersecurity protects and why it matters.

video.title: Cyber Security Full Course 2026

steps: Write down three things you want to protect: your money, your photos, your accounts.
List three ways each one could be stolen or damaged.
Learn the three goals of security: confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Find one recent news story about a hack and write down what went wrong.
days.task: Write a short note: what cybersecurity is, in your own words, and why it matters to you.
days.challenge: Ask a friend what they do to stay safe online and compare it with your list.

options: People, their data, their money and the systems they use
quiz.explain: Cybersecurity protects people and their data, money and devices from theft, damage and spying.

quiz.q: What are the three goals of security?
quiz.explain: The CIA triad: keep data private (confidentiality), correct (integrity) and reachable when needed (availability).

options: Everyone who uses a phone, email or the internet
quiz.explain: Anyone online is a target. Attackers go after ordinary people because their defences are usually weaker.

days.title: How Hackers Think
days.goal: Learn the main types of attacks so you can recognise them.

video.title: Cybersecurity Engineer Full Course 2026

steps: Learn five attack types: phishing, malware, ransomware, social engineering and password attacks.
For each one, write down what the attacker wants and how they get it.
Learn the difference between a hacker, a cracker and an ethical hacker.
Find one example of each attack type in the news.
days.task: Make a one-page guide to the five attack types with a real example for each.
days.challenge: Explain to a friend, in simple words, what ransomware does.

options: A fake message that tricks you into giving away passwords or money
quiz.explain: Phishing is a fake email or message that looks real and tricks you into clicking a bad link or sharing secrets.

options: Malware that locks your files and demands money to unlock them
quiz.explain: Ransomware encrypts your files so you cannot open them, then demands payment for the key.

options: A security professional who tests systems with permission to find and fix weaknesses
quiz.explain: Ethical hackers attack systems legally, with permission, to find holes before criminals do.

days.title: Passwords That Actually Protect You
days.goal: Make strong, unique passwords and store them safely.

video.title: Cyber Security Course 2026 [FREE]

steps: Check if your passwords are reused: list your accounts and mark any that share a password.
Make a strong password: at least 12 characters, mixed letters, numbers and symbols.
Use a passphrase: four random words joined together, like 'correct horse battery staple'.
Install a password manager and move your first five passwords into it.
days.task: Move all your important accounts into a password manager with a unique password each.
days.challenge: Change the password of your email account to a strong, unique one.

options: Long, random and unique to one account
quiz.explain: A strong password is long, random and used for only one account, so one leak cannot unlock everything.

options: Because one leaked password gives attackers the key to every account that shares it
quiz.explain: Attackers try leaked passwords on many sites. Reuse turns one breach into many.

options: An app that creates and stores strong unique passwords for you, protected by one master password
quiz.explain: A password manager remembers all your passwords, so you only need to remember one strong master password.

days.title: Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)
days.goal: Add a second lock to your accounts with 2FA.

video.title: Learn Complete Cyber Security Course Free 2026

steps: Learn what 2FA is: something you know (password) plus something you have (phone or key).
Turn on 2FA for your email account using an authenticator app.
Turn on 2FA for your bank and your main social media accounts.
Save your backup codes in a safe place, not on your phone.
days.task: Turn on 2FA for your three most important accounts and save the backup codes.
days.challenge: Test logging in with 2FA to make sure it works.

options: A second check after your password, like a code from your phone
quiz.explain: 2FA asks for a second proof, like a code from an app, so a stolen password alone is not enough.

quiz.q: Which is safer: a code by text message or an authenticator app?
options: An authenticator app, because text messages can be intercepted
quiz.explain: Authenticator apps are safer. Text codes can be stolen by SIM swap attacks.

options: So you can still get in if you lose your phone
quiz.explain: Backup codes are your spare key. Without them, losing your phone can lock you out of your account.

days.title: Phishing: Spot the Fake
days.goal: Recognise phishing emails and messages before you click.

video.title: CyberSecurity Full Course 2027

steps: Learn the five signs of phishing: urgency, strange sender, bad spelling, odd links and requests for secrets.
Open your spam folder and find one phishing email. List the signs it shows.
Hover over a link (do not click) to see where it really goes.
Practise: write down what you would do if your bank emailed you about a problem.
days.task: Find three phishing signs in a real spam email and write them down.
days.challenge: Show a friend a phishing email and ask them to spot the signs.

quiz.q: What is the most common sign of phishing?
options: Urgency: 'Act now or your account will close!'
quiz.explain: Phishing creates panic so you act without thinking. Real companies rarely demand instant action by email.

quiz.q: What should you do with a suspicious link?
options: Hover to see the real address, and go to the site yourself instead of clicking
quiz.explain: Never click a suspicious link. Type the site's address yourself or use the app you already have.

quiz.q: What should you do if you clicked a phishing link?
options: Change your password, turn on 2FA and check your accounts
quiz.explain: Act fast: change the password, turn on 2FA and check for strange activity.

days.title: Safe Browsing and Public Wi-Fi
days.goal: Stay safe when you browse and when you use public Wi-Fi.

video.title: How to get better security than passwords alone

steps: Check that websites you log into start with https and show a padlock.
Turn on your browser's safe browsing and pop-up blocker.
Learn why public Wi-Fi is risky: anyone on it can watch unprotected traffic.
Use a VPN or your phone data for banking on public Wi-Fi.
days.task: Check the five sites you use most and confirm they use https.
days.challenge: Turn off automatic Wi-Fi connection on your phone so it does not join unknown networks.

options: The connection between you and the site is encrypted
quiz.explain: https encrypts your connection, so others on the same network cannot read what you send.

options: Because anyone on the same network can try to watch or intercept unprotected traffic
quiz.explain: Public Wi-Fi is shared. Attackers on it can snoop on traffic that is not encrypted.

options: It encrypts your internet traffic and hides it from the local network
quiz.explain: A VPN encrypts your traffic, so even on public Wi-Fi, snoops cannot read it.

days.title: Project 1: Personal Security Audit
days.goal: Audit your own digital life and fix the biggest risks.

video.title: Passwords, Password Managers & 2FA: Full Setup Walkthrough

steps: List all your important accounts: email, bank, social media, shopping.
Check each one: is the password unique and strong? Is 2FA on?
Check your phone: is the screen lock on, is the software updated?
Write a fix list and complete the top five fixes.
days.task: Finish your security audit and fix the top five risks you found.
days.challenge: Teach one family member how to turn on 2FA.

options: A check of your accounts, devices and habits to find and fix risks
quiz.explain: An audit is a review: what do you have, what protects it, and what is still weak?

options: A unique password and 2FA on your email, because email resets everything else
quiz.explain: Your email can reset most other accounts. Protecting it with a unique password and 2FA protects everything.

quiz.q: Why update your phone and apps?
options: Because updates fix security holes attackers use
quiz.explain: Updates patch holes. Attackers target people who skip them.

project.title: Personal Security Audit
project.brief: Audit your own digital life: list your important accounts, check each one for a unique strong password and 2FA, check your phone's lock and updates, and fix the top five risks you find.
checks: You listed all your important accounts.
Each account was checked for a unique strong password.
2FA is on for your three most important accounts.
Your phone has a screen lock and is updated.
The top five risks you found are fixed.
You taught one person how to turn on 2FA.

days.title: Malware: Viruses, Ransomware and Spyware
days.goal: Learn what malware is, how it spreads and how to stop it.

video.title: Harvard CS50's Intro to Cybersecurity – Full University Course

steps: Learn the main types: virus, worm, trojan, spyware and ransomware.
Learn how malware spreads: bad downloads, email attachments and fake updates.
Install a trusted antivirus and run a full scan.
Learn what to do if your computer starts acting strangely.
days.task: Run a full antivirus scan on your computer and check the result.
days.challenge: Find one program on your computer you do not recognise and check what it is.

options: Malware that pretends to be a useful program to trick you into installing it
quiz.explain: A trojan hides inside something that looks harmless, like a free game or a fake update.

quiz.q: How does most malware get onto computers?
options: Through downloads, email attachments and fake updates that users open
quiz.explain: Most malware needs you to open it. A bad download or attachment is the usual way in.

options: Malware that secretly watches what you do and steals information
quiz.explain: Spyware hides on your device and records what you type, where you go and what you do.

days.title: Networks: How the Internet Moves Data
days.goal: Understand IP addresses, DNS and how data travels.

video.title: Hands-On Cybersecurity and Ethical Hacking – Full Course

steps: Learn what an IP address is: your device's address on the network.
Learn what DNS does: it turns names like google.com into IP addresses.
Use ping to check if a website is reachable.
Use ipconfig or ifconfig to see your own IP address.
days.task: Find your IP address, ping three websites and write down the results.
days.challenge: Explain DNS to a friend in one sentence.

options: A number that identifies a device on a network
quiz.explain: An IP address is like a home address for your device. It tells the network where to send data.

options: It turns website names into IP addresses
quiz.explain: DNS is the internet's phone book. You type a name, DNS finds the number.

options: A small chunk of data that travels across the network
quiz.explain: Data travels in packets: small pieces that are sent separately and put back together at the other end.

days.title: Firewalls and What They Block
days.goal: Understand firewalls and check yours is on.

video.title: Computer Networking Fundamentals Course

steps: Learn what a firewall does: it blocks unwanted connections to your computer.
Check that your computer's firewall is turned on.
Learn the difference between inbound and outbound rules.
Block one program from the internet in your firewall settings.
days.task: Check your firewall is on and list the programs allowed through it.
days.challenge: Turn off any program you do not recognise in the firewall list.

options: A barrier that controls which network connections can reach your computer
quiz.explain: A firewall watches network traffic and blocks connections that are not allowed.

quiz.q: What is the difference between inbound and outbound?
options: Inbound is traffic coming in, outbound is traffic going out
quiz.explain: Inbound rules control what can connect to you. Outbound rules control what your computer can connect to.

quiz.q: Why block a program in the firewall?
options: To stop a suspicious program from sending your data out
quiz.explain: Blocking a suspicious program stops it from sending data to the internet.

days.title: Linux Basics for Security
days.goal: Learn the Linux basics every security learner needs.

video.title: Introduction to Linux – Full Course for Beginners

steps: Install a Linux virtual machine with VirtualBox and Ubuntu or Kali.
Learn to move around: pwd, ls, cd and mkdir.
Learn to read files: cat, less and head.
Learn to check who you are and what is running: whoami and ps.
days.task: Set up your Linux virtual machine and practise the basic commands.
days.challenge: Create a folder, make a file in it and read it back.

quiz.q: Why do security learners use Linux?
options: Because most security tools are built for Linux
quiz.explain: Most security tools, like Nmap and Wireshark, are made for Linux first.

options: It lists the files in a folder
quiz.explain: ls lists what is in the current folder.

options: It shows the folder you are in
quiz.explain: pwd prints the working directory: the folder you are currently in.

days.title: The Command Line: Your First Lab
days.goal: Get comfortable with the terminal and file permissions.

video.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - Full Course 2026

steps: Learn file permissions: read, write and execute for owner, group and others.
Change permissions with chmod and see the effect.
Use sudo to run a command as the administrator.
Find a file with find and search inside files with grep.
days.task: Change the permissions of a test file and check who can read it.
days.challenge: Use grep to find a word inside a log file.

options: Rules that say who can read, write or run a file
quiz.explain: Permissions control who can read, change or run a file. They stop the wrong people touching important files.

options: It runs a command with administrator power
quiz.explain: sudo runs a command as the administrator, which is needed for system changes.

options: It searches inside files for lines that match a pattern
quiz.explain: grep finds lines containing a word or pattern, which is handy for reading logs.

days.title: Virtual Machines and Safe Labs
days.goal: Build a safe lab where you can practise without breaking anything.

video.title: Can you find the bug? JavaScript security vulnerabilities course

steps: Install VirtualBox on your computer.
Create a virtual machine and install Ubuntu or Kali Linux in it.
Take a snapshot so you can undo any mistake.
Set the network to NAT or host-only so the lab stays separate from your real network.
days.task: Build your lab virtual machine and take a snapshot.
days.challenge: Break something in the lab on purpose, then restore the snapshot.

options: A computer running inside your computer, separate from your real system
quiz.explain: A virtual machine is a computer in software. It runs inside your real computer but is separate from it.

quiz.q: Why practise in a virtual machine?
options: Because mistakes stay inside the lab and cannot harm your real computer
quiz.explain: A lab VM is a safe sandbox. You can break things, test tools and learn without risking your real system.

options: A saved state of a virtual machine you can return to at any time
quiz.explain: A snapshot saves the VM's exact state. You can roll back to it after a mistake.

days.title: Project 2: Set Up a Safe Home Lab
days.goal: Build a safe home lab with a Linux VM and the basic security tools.

video.title: Cyber Security Full Course 2026

steps: Install VirtualBox and a Linux virtual machine.
Install Wireshark, Nmap and a text editor in the VM.
Take a snapshot of the clean VM.
Write a one-page guide to your lab: what is installed and how to restore it.
days.task: Finish your home lab and test that Wireshark and Nmap run.
days.challenge: Show your lab guide to one person and explain what each tool does.

quiz.q: Why take a snapshot of a clean lab?
options: So you can always return to a known-good state after experiments
quiz.explain: A clean snapshot is your reset button. After any experiment, you can go back to a fresh lab.

options: It scans a network to find devices and open ports
quiz.explain: Nmap probes a network and reports which devices are there and which services they offer.

quiz.q: Why keep the lab separate from your real network?
options: So experiments cannot touch your real computers or data
quiz.explain: A separate lab network stops your experiments from reaching your real devices.

project.title: Set Up a Safe Home Lab
project.brief: Build a safe home lab: install VirtualBox and a Linux virtual machine, install Wireshark and Nmap, take a snapshot of the clean VM, and write a one-page guide to your lab.
checks: VirtualBox and a Linux VM are installed.
Wireshark and Nmap run in the VM.
A snapshot of the clean VM exists.
The lab network is separate from your real network.
A one-page lab guide exists.
You can explain what each tool does.

days.title: Wireshark: Watching Network Traffic
days.goal: Capture and read network traffic with Wireshark.

video.title: Cybersecurity Engineer Full Course 2026

steps: Open Wireshark and start a capture on your network interface.
Visit a website and watch the packets appear.
Filter the capture to show only DNS traffic.
Find one packet and read its source and destination addresses.
days.task: Capture traffic for one minute and find the top three websites your computer talked to.
days.challenge: Filter for HTTP traffic and read one request.

options: A tool that captures and shows network traffic packet by packet
quiz.explain: Wireshark records the packets on your network and lets you inspect them.

quiz.q: What is a filter in Wireshark?
options: A rule that shows only the packets you care about, like dns or http
quiz.explain: Filters hide the noise. Type 'dns' and you see only DNS packets.

quiz.q: Is it legal to capture traffic?
options: Only on networks you own or have permission to test
quiz.explain: Capture only on your own network or with clear permission. Capturing others' traffic without permission is illegal.

days.title: Password Attacks and How to Stop Them
days.goal: Learn how passwords are attacked and how to defend them.

video.title: Cyber Security Course 2026 [FREE]

steps: Learn three attacks: brute force, dictionary and credential stuffing.
Learn what hashing is: passwords are stored as scrambled values, not plain text.
Learn why long passwords beat complex short ones.
Check if your email has appeared in a breach.
days.task: Check your email on a breach-checking site and change any password that was leaked.
days.challenge: Turn on 2FA everywhere a leaked password was found.

quiz.q: What is a brute force attack?
options: Trying every possible password until one works
Stealing a password from a sticky note
quiz.explain: Brute force tries passwords one by one. Long passwords make this take years instead of minutes.

options: Trying passwords leaked from one site on many other sites
quiz.explain: Credential stuffing reuses leaked passwords on other sites, which is why reusing passwords is so dangerous.

options: Scrambling a password into a fixed value that cannot be turned back
quiz.explain: Hashing turns a password into a scrambled value. The site checks your password by hashing it and comparing, never storing the real password.

days.title: Web Security: How Websites Get Hacked
days.goal: Learn the most common web attacks and how to spot them.

video.title: Learn Complete Cyber Security Course Free 2026

steps: Learn SQL injection: when user input is pasted into a database query.
Learn cross-site scripting (XSS): when an attacker injects code into a page.
Learn how to spot a vulnerable form: try a quote mark and watch the error.
Learn why sites must check and clean all user input.
days.task: Find the OWASP Top 10 list and write a one-line summary of each item.
days.challenge: Explain SQL injection to a friend in simple words.

options: An attack where a user types SQL into a form and the site runs it
quiz.explain: SQL injection happens when input is pasted into a query. A crafted input can change the query and steal data.

options: An attack where bad code is injected into a web page and runs in other users' browsers
quiz.explain: XSS injects scripts into a page. When others visit, the script runs in their browser and can steal their session.

options: A list of the best websites
A list of the ten most serious web security risks, updated regularly
quiz.explain: The OWASP Top 10 is the standard list of the most common and dangerous web security problems.

days.title: Social Engineering
days.goal: Learn how attackers trick people, not computers.

video.title: CyberSecurity Full Course 2027

steps: Learn the main tricks: urgency, authority, curiosity and fear.
Learn what pretexting is: making up a story to get information.
Practise saying no to a suspicious request, even from someone who sounds official.
Write a rule for yourself: never share a password or code with anyone.
days.task: Write down three social engineering tricks and how you would respond to each.
days.challenge: Test a friend: send them a suspicious message and see if they spot it.

options: Tricking people into giving away secrets or access, instead of hacking computers
quiz.explain: Social engineering attacks people, not machines. It uses trust, fear and urgency to get secrets.

options: Making up a believable story to trick someone into sharing information
quiz.explain: Pretexting is a made-up scenario, like pretending to be IT support, to get someone to share information.

options: Because it uses normal human instincts: trust, helpfulness and fear
quiz.explain: It works because it targets human nature. Being helpful and trusting is normal, and attackers exploit it.

days.title: Encryption: How Secrets Stay Secret
days.goal: Understand encryption and how it protects data.

video.title: How to get better security than passwords alone

steps: Learn what encryption does: it scrambles data so only the right key can read it.
Learn the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption.
Learn what HTTPS does for your browsing.
Check that your messaging apps use end-to-end encryption.
days.task: Check three apps you use and confirm which ones use end-to-end encryption.
days.challenge: Explain encryption to a friend using the locked-box analogy.

options: Scrambling data with a key so only someone with the key can read it
quiz.explain: Encryption turns readable data into scrambled data. Only the key turns it back.

quiz.q: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
options: Symmetric uses one shared key, asymmetric uses a public key and a private key
quiz.explain: Symmetric encryption shares one key. Asymmetric uses a public key to lock and a private key to unlock.

options: Encryption where only the sender and receiver can read the messages, not even the app company
quiz.explain: End-to-end encryption means only the two people talking can read the messages. The service in the middle cannot.

days.title: Backups and Recovery
days.goal: Protect yourself from ransomware and accidents with backups.

video.title: Passwords, Password Managers & 2FA: Full Setup Walkthrough

steps: Follow the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, two different places, one offsite.
Back up your important files to an external drive or cloud.
Test the backup by restoring one file.
Set a reminder to back up every week.
days.task: Back up your important files and test restoring one of them.
days.challenge: Write down your backup plan: what, where and how often.

options: Three copies of data, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy offsite
quiz.explain: 3-2-1 means three copies, two different media, one offsite. If one copy fails, others survive.

options: Because a backup you cannot restore is useless
quiz.explain: Untested backups often fail when you need them. Restoring one file proves the backup works.

options: So a fire, flood or theft at home cannot destroy all copies at once
quiz.explain: An offsite copy survives disasters at home. If all copies are in one place, one disaster takes them all.

days.title: Project 3: Secure a Small Business
days.goal: Do a security review for a small business and write a plan to fix it.

video.title: Harvard CS50's Intro to Cybersecurity – Full University Course

steps: Pick a small business, real or imaginary, with a website, email and a few computers.
List its assets: what data, money and systems does it have?
List its risks: phishing, ransomware, weak passwords, no backups.
Write a security plan with ten fixes, ordered by importance.
days.task: Finish the security plan with ten fixes and a short explanation for each.
days.challenge: Present the plan to one person in under three minutes.

options: Listing what you have, what could go wrong, and how likely and bad each risk is
quiz.explain: A risk assessment lists assets, threats and how bad each one would be, so you fix the worst first.

quiz.q: Which fix comes first for a small business?
options: Unique passwords, 2FA and backups, because they stop the most common attacks
quiz.explain: The basics stop most attacks: unique passwords, 2FA and backups. Expensive tools come later.

quiz.q: What makes a security plan good?
options: It is clear, ordered by importance, and each fix has a reason
quiz.explain: A good plan is short, clear and ordered. Each fix explains what it stops and why it matters.

project.title: Secure a Small Business
project.brief: Do a security review for a small business: list its assets and risks, then write a security plan with ten fixes ordered by importance, with a short explanation for each.
checks: The business's assets are listed.
The risks are listed with phishing, ransomware and weak passwords covered.
The plan has ten fixes.
The fixes are ordered by importance.
Each fix has a short explanation.
You can present the plan in under three minutes.

days.title: Ethical Hacking Tools Overview
days.goal: Meet the main tools ethical hackers use, and when each one fits.

video.title: Hands-On Cybersecurity and Ethical Hacking – Full Course

steps: Learn what Nmap, Wireshark, Burp Suite and Metasploit are for.
Install one tool in your lab and run it against your own VM.
Learn the rule: only test systems you own or have written permission to test.
Write a one-line summary of each tool's job.
days.task: Install one new tool in your lab and test it against your own virtual machine.
days.challenge: Write a short guide: which tool to use for which job.

options: Testing web applications for security holes
quiz.explain: Burp Suite sits between your browser and a website, letting you inspect and change requests to find web flaws.

options: A framework for testing known vulnerabilities safely
quiz.explain: Metasploit is a toolkit for testing whether known vulnerabilities can be exploited, used by professionals with permission.

quiz.q: Why only test systems you own or have permission for?
options: Because testing without permission is illegal and can be treated as a crime
quiz.explain: Unauthorised testing is illegal, even with good intentions. Always get written permission first.

days.title: Nmap: Finding Devices on a Network
days.goal: Scan a network with Nmap and read the results.

video.title: Computer Networking Fundamentals Course

steps: Run a simple scan of your lab network with nmap 192.168.1.0/24.
List the devices Nmap found and their open ports.
Scan one device in detail to see which services it runs.
Save the results to a file for your notes.
days.task: Scan your lab network and write down every device and open port you find.
days.challenge: Close one port you do not need on your own VM.

options: It scans networks to find devices, open ports and services
quiz.explain: Nmap probes a network and reports which devices are there and what services they offer.

options: A numbered door on a computer that a service listens on, like port 80 for websites
quiz.explain: A port is a numbered endpoint. Services listen on ports: 80 for web, 22 for SSH, 443 for secure web.

quiz.q: Why close ports you do not need?
options: Because every open port is a possible way in for an attacker
quiz.explain: Open ports are doors. Every open door is a chance for an attacker, so close the ones you do not use.

days.title: Incident Response: What to Do When Hacked
days.goal: Learn the steps to take when something goes wrong.

video.title: Introduction to Linux – Full Course for Beginners

steps: Learn the six steps: prepare, detect, contain, remove, recover, learn.
Practise the first step: disconnect the affected device from the network.
Learn what evidence to save before you clean up.
Write a one-page incident plan for your own computer.
days.task: Write your personal incident plan: what to do first, who to call, what to save.
days.challenge: Practise the plan with a pretend incident: a suspicious email you clicked.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do when you suspect a hack?
options: Disconnect from the network to stop the spread, then assess
quiz.explain: Disconnecting stops the attacker from reaching more devices and stops data leaving.

quiz.q: Why save evidence before cleaning up?
options: So you can work out what happened and prove it if needed
quiz.explain: Logs and files show what the attacker did. Cleaning up first destroys the clues.

quiz.q: What is the last step of incident response?
options: Learn from it: fix the hole and update your defences
quiz.explain: After recovery, learn from the incident: fix the weakness so it cannot happen again the same way.

days.title: Security for Small Business
days.goal: Apply what you learned to protect a small business.

video.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - Full Course 2026

steps: List the five most common attacks on small businesses.
Write a simple password policy: unique passwords, a manager, 2FA.
Write a backup rule and a software update rule.
Write a one-page staff guide: how to spot phishing and what to do.
days.task: Write a one-page security guide for a small business.
days.challenge: Teach one person the three signs of phishing.

options: Because their defences are usually weaker and they still hold valuable data
quiz.explain: Attackers target small businesses because they are easier to break into than big companies, and their data is still valuable.

options: Simple rules for passwords: unique, long, in a manager, with 2FA
quiz.explain: A password policy is a short set of rules everyone follows, so passwords stop being the weak link.

options: Because staff are the first line of defence: one click can open the door
quiz.explain: Most breaches start with one person clicking one bad link. Training turns staff into a defence, not a weakness.

days.title: Careers in Cybersecurity and Certifications
days.goal: Learn how to turn these skills into a job.

video.title: Can you find the bug? JavaScript security vulnerabilities course

steps: List the main job roles: analyst, penetration tester, engineer and consultant.
Learn what CompTIA Security+, CEH and CISSP are for.
Find one entry-level job advert and list the skills it asks for.
Write a plan for your next three months of learning.
days.task: Find three entry-level cybersecurity jobs and list the skills they ask for.
days.challenge: Pick one certification to aim for and write your study plan.

quiz.q: What does a security analyst do?
options: Watches for threats, investigates alerts and helps fix problems
quiz.explain: A security analyst monitors systems, checks alerts and investigates anything suspicious.
Security+ is a popular first certification. It proves you know the basics of security.

quiz.q: What matters most for a first security job?
options: Hands-on skills, a lab, and proof you can find and fix problems
quiz.explain: Employers want proof you can do the work: a home lab, projects and clear explanations beat a pile of certificates.

days.title: Security+ Study Plan
days.goal: Plan your study for the CompTIA Security+ exam.

video.title: Cyber Security Full Course 2026

steps: List the five Security+ domains and what each covers.
Rate yourself on each domain from 1 to 5.
Pick your weakest domain and study it for one hour.
Do ten practice questions and check your answers.
days.task: Write your Security+ study plan with a date for each domain.
days.challenge: Do twenty practice questions and note your score.

options: The five areas the exam covers: attacks, architecture, operations, governance and security program management
quiz.explain: Security+ has five domains. Knowing what each covers tells you what to study.

options: So you spend study time on your weakest areas, not your strongest
quiz.explain: Rating yourself shows where to focus. Studying what you already know wastes time.

quiz.q: How should you use practice questions?
options: Do them, check why each answer is right or wrong, and learn the idea behind it
quiz.explain: Practice questions teach you the ideas. Understanding why an answer is right matters more than the score.

days.title: Staying Safe on Social Media
days.goal: Protect yourself on social media: privacy settings and oversharing.

video.title: Cybersecurity Engineer Full Course 2026

steps: Check the privacy settings on your main social media accounts.
Turn off location sharing on your posts.
Learn what oversharing is: posting details attackers can use, like your birthday or your school.
Review your friend list and remove people you do not know.
days.task: Lock down your social media privacy settings and remove one piece of overshared information.
days.challenge: Turn off location tags on your photos.

options: Posting personal details that attackers can use to guess passwords or trick you
quiz.explain: Oversharing gives attackers facts: your birthday, your pet's name, your school. Those facts answer security questions.

options: So strangers cannot see where you are or where you live
quiz.explain: Location tags tell strangers where you are right now, and patterns in them can reveal where you live or work.

options: Because fake accounts use friend requests to see your posts and learn about you
quiz.explain: Fake accounts send friend requests to see private posts. Only accept people you actually know.

days.title: Privacy: Your Data, Your Rules
days.goal: Understand what data companies collect and how to limit it.

video.title: Cyber Security Course 2026 [FREE]

steps: Check what permissions your apps have and remove the ones they do not need.
Turn off ad tracking on your phone.
Learn what cookies do and clear the ones you do not need.
Use a private browser window for searches you do not want saved.
days.task: Review your app permissions and remove at least three you do not need.
days.challenge: Clear your browser cookies and check what changes.

options: The access an app has to your camera, location, contacts and files
quiz.explain: Permissions let apps use your camera, location or contacts. Many apps ask for more than they need.

options: They remember you: logins, settings and what you looked at
quiz.explain: Cookies store small bits of data in your browser so sites remember you. They also let advertisers track you.

options: Because every piece of data collected can be leaked, sold or misused
quiz.explain: Data you do not share cannot be leaked. Limiting collection reduces what can go wrong.

days.title: Capstone Prep: Plan Your Security Project
days.goal: Review everything, pick your capstone project and plan your demo.

video.title: Learn Complete Cyber Security Course Free 2026

steps: List the projects you did and pick the strongest one to finish.
Write a short plan: the problem, the audit, the fixes and the demo.
Practise explaining your work in simple words, as if to a friend.
Record a short video or write a short post showing your lab or your audit.
days.task: Write your capstone plan and a one-minute explanation of your project.
days.challenge: Show your project to one person and note their questions, then improve it.

quiz.q: What makes a good capstone security project?
options: A real audit or lab with clear findings and fixes that make something safer
quiz.explain: A good capstone finds real risks, fixes them, and shows the before and after clearly.

options: Because explaining simply proves you truly understand it
quiz.explain: If you can explain your work in simple words, you really understand it. That is what employers look for.

quiz.q: What should your capstone plan include?
options: The problem, the audit or lab, the fixes and how you will show it
quiz.explain: A plan covers the problem, what you will audit or build, the fixes you will make and how you will present it.

capstone.title: Audit and Secure a Real System
capstone.brief: Pick a real system to secure: your own digital life, a family member's, or a small business. Do a full audit, fix the risks, set up a safe lab to test your fixes, and present a before-and-after report with a short demo.
checks: The project covers a real system and you can explain what it is in one sentence.
A full audit lists the assets, risks and current protections.
The top risks are fixed: unique passwords, 2FA, updates and backups.
A safe lab was used to test at least one fix.
A before-and-after report shows what changed.
The report includes a short demo or screenshots.
You can present the project in under five minutes in simple words.
deliverables: A written audit report with assets, risks and fixes.
A before-and-after comparison of the security state.
A safe lab setup with a guide.
A short demo video or screenshots of your work.
A one-page write-up of what you learned in 30 days.
